papers.title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
papers.abstract: Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.

papers.title: Syntaxin-1 and syntaxin binding protein 1-1 are required for planarian behavior and brain regeneration
papers.abstract: Background: Nervous system regeneration requires creation of new neurons and their integration into new and existing networks. How new neurons find their targets and reconnect in the environment of regenerating tissue remains a major gap in knowledge. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is well suited to the study of neural regeneration due to the remarkable ability of planarians to regenerate their entire body, including the nervous system. However, we have not yet been able to explore synaptogenesis in regeneration using planarians due to a lack of tools to study synapses. Here we investigate potential players in planarian synapse, focusing on the conserved syntaxin protein family, which functions in neurotransmitter vesicle fusion at the synapse. Results: We found that reduction of either syntaxin-1 (stx1) or syntaxin-binding protein 1-1 (stxbp1-1) decreased locomotion and impeded brain regeneration, specifically in synapse-rich regions. Conclusions: Our observations support STX-1 and STXBP1-1 as bona fide synapse components, providing a starting point for studies neuronal connectivity during homeostatic remodeling and regeneration.

papers.title: Astrocyte-Specific dsRNA-ADAR1 Signalling Links Innate Immunity to Complement Activation in Parkinson Disease
papers.abstract: Background: Dysregulated innate immune activation is a key feature of Parkinson disease (PD), but the upstream triggers and cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unclear. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) has emerged as a potential driver of innate immune responses. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1), particularly its interferon-inducible p150 isoform, edits dsRNA to limit aberrant immune activation. Whether this dsRNA-ADAR1 axis contributes to neuroinflammation in PD in a cell-type-specific manner is unknown. Methods: We performed immunofluorescence on post-mortem cingulate cortex tissue from PD cases and controls to localise dsRNA, ADAR1 p150 and pathological alpha-synuclein protein. We integrated these findings with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from three independent human brain datasets. An eight-module gene scoring framework was applied to assess dsRNA processing, sensing, and downstream innate immune pathways in neurons and astrocytes. Results: In PD cortex, the proportion of dsRNA-positive astrocytes was higher than in controls, whereas neuronal dsRNA positivity did not differ between groups. ADAR1 p150 positivity increased in both astrocytes and neurons, and the proportion of ADAR1 p150 positive astrocytes correlated with astrocytic -synuclein burden. Transcriptomic analyses showed that neurons were enriched for dsRNA editing and processing machinery, whereas astrocytes exhibited higher expression of dsRNA sensing pathways, innate immune responses, and transposable element control. While overall pathway activity did not differ between PD and controls after covariate adjustment, network analyses revealed cell-type-specific coupling patterns. Notably, complement gene expression showed a strong and selective association with dsRNA-related pathways in astrocytes, whereas interferon and NF-{kappa}B signalling were shared across cell types. In both cell types, ADAR1-associated gene programmes were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation and PD-related pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify astrocytes as a central site of relative dsRNA accumulation and ADAR1 p150 induction in the PD cortex. The selective coupling of dsRNA sensing to complement activation in astrocytes highlights a cell-type-specific innate immune pathway that is constitutively present rather than induced by disease. Together, our protein-level and network-level findings converge on a coherent and testable model in which a constitutive astrocytic circuit is engaged by disease-associated dsRNA accumulation, with potential relevance for disease progression and therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of Starburst Amacrine Cells
papers.abstract: During mammalian nervous system development, multipotent progenitor cells differentiate into hundreds of distinct neuronal subtypes. Neuronal subtype terminal differentiation is regulated by transcription factors that directly control the acquisition and maintenance of terminal identity. Using the mouse retina as a model system, we show that the transcription factor ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of starburst amacrine cells (SACs), the sole cholinergic neuron subtype in the retina. We conditionally deleted Isl1 selectively from amacrine and horizontal cell precursors, allowing us to assess its cell-autonomous role in SAC development without disrupting its critical function in bipolar cell and retinal ganglion cell development. We find that ISL1 is not required for initial SAC specification but is required for their terminal differentiation. Isl1-deficient SACs retain a GABAergic amacrine cell identity but fail to adopt many SAC-specific features including expression of genes required for cholinergic transmission. In the absence of ISL1, SACs fail to migrate properly, with both OFF- and ON- SACs localizing to the inner nuclear layer. Deletion of Isl1 from post-migratory SACs at later stages of development revealed that it is also required for maintaining SAC identity and proper dendrite stratification. Loss of Isl1 from SACs ultimately caused abnormal development of the direction selective circuit. Together, these findings establish that ISL1 is required for the induction and maintenance of SAC-specific identity from a generic amacrine state.

papers.title: Motor effort biases perceptual decisions through later-stage evidence accumulation rather than early sensory-attentional processing
papers.abstract: Motor effort has been shown to bias perceptual decisions toward less effortful choices, but it remains unknown whether this bias already takes effect during the early stages of decision formation through preparatory attentional allocation or sensory processing, or during later-stage evidence accumulation preceding response execution. This study investigated when motor effort becomes integrated into decision formation by focusing on the temporal evolution of neural processing during perceptual decision-making. While 64-channel EEG was recorded, twenty-four healthy adults performed an orientation discrimination task in which two Gabor patches appeared simultaneously in the left and right visual hemifield and decisions were reported using two pressure-sensitive response buttons requiring different levels of force. We found that motor effort modulated EEG activity at both the preparatory and later decision stages: pre-stimulus alpha power was reduced over the occipito-parietal cortex contralateral to the low-effort option, and mean centro-parietal positivity (CPP) amplitude preceding response execution was greater over centro-parietal cortex for low-effort choices, while leaving early sensory representations intact as indicated by no differences in P1 or N1 amplitude following stimulus onset. Trial-by-trial CPP amplitude preceding response execution increased with the likelihood of selecting the low-effort option, whereas the pre-stimulus alpha modulation was not associated with behavioral decision bias. These findings suggest that motor effort biases perceptual decisions primarily during later-stage evidence accumulation, thereby providing insight into the neural basis of embodied perceptual decision making.

papers.title: Astrocytes in the Dentate Gyrus Shift the Equilibrium from Pattern Separation to Pattern Completion and Inhibit Fear Extinction
papers.abstract: Pattern separation and pattern completion are core hippocampal computations linked to memory interference and overgeneralization in many neuropsychiatric disorders and to mnemonic discrimination deficits in neurodegenerative conditions. Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important integrators and modulators of neuronal activity as many studies have shown changes in animal behavior and neural circuits induced by manipulation of astrocytic activity. The role of astrocytes in the dentate gyrus for learning and memory is, however, largely unknown. To investigate the functional significance of astrocytic activity in the dentate gyrus, we expressed the calcium extruding pump hPMCA2w/b (CalEx), resulting in inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity, the Gq-coupled receptor hM3Dq, or the Gi-coupled receptor hM4Di, allowing chronic activation of Gq- and Gi-dependent pathways by a designer drug, in dentate gyrus astrocytes. Our main finding is that inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity by CalEx resulted in improved pattern separation and impaired pattern completion. In -vivo calcium imaging revealed that CalEx expression in astrocytes altered the neuronal activity pattern in dentate gyrus neurons with an overall inhibitory effect. This suggests that in the dentate gyrus astrocytes promote the activity of these neurons. Furthermore, chronic activation of hM4Di resulted in impaired between-session fear extinction while chronic activation of hM3Dq resulted in impaired within-session fear extinction and improved pattern separation learning over multiple days, suggesting that activation of astrocytic activity enhances mechanistically separable forms of fear extinction in a Gq- or Gi-pathway-specific manner. Our findings reveal that dentate gyrus astrocytic calcium shifts the balance between pattern separation and pattern completion towards pattern completion and thus modulates an essential neuronal functional output of the dentate gyrus. Chronic activation of astrocytes inhibits fear extinction, and thus also affects management of memory interference. Our findings imply that astrocytic modulation may be beneficial to treat cognitive deficits in disorders in which overgeneralization is a problem.

papers.title: Nicotinic modulation of frontal circuits breaks the cycle of attentional performance failure
papers.abstract: The ability to recover from consecutive failures is critical for adaptive behavior, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. In vivo screening of neuromodulatory inputs onto frontal-sensory cognitive control circuit identified a frontal cholinergic mechanism that counteracts lapses in attentional engagement following repeated errors. Cholinergic input from the basal forebrain to the frontal cortex was necessary and sufficient to restore performance after errors, specifically after repeated-but not after a single-failure. This effect was mediated by 7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in frontal-sensory cortical neurons, which sustained cortical circuit activity and frontal-sensory cortical oscillations during attentional engagement. Targeted optogenetic activation of these frontal-sensory neurons disrupted cycles of attentional performance failure and reinstated behavioral performance in a mouse model of neuropsychiatric syndrome. These findings reveal a circuit-level mechanism of cholinergic control that confers cognitive resilience under conditions of persistent failure.

papers.title: An integrated multi-omic atlas of the choroid plexus highlights conserved molecular programs of epithelial function
papers.abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) is a specialized epithelial tissue responsible for production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), maintenance of the blood-CSF barrier and regulation of CSF-borne signaling factors. However, despite the ChP's central role in CSF homeostasis, conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial function across species and conditions remain incompletely defined. In this study, we integrated eight mouse and human single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq datasets to build a multi-species ChP atlas capturing major epithelial, stromal, vascular, and immune populations. Cross-dataset differential expression identified a conserved epithelial gene program encompassing ion transport, barrier function, ciliogenesis, and secretory signaling, while prioritizing understudied genes including CLIC6 and VAT1L. Co-expression network analysis resolved conserved epithelial meta-programs, and transcription factor regulatory inference identified OTX2, MSX1, and GLIS3 among conserved regulators of epithelial gene expression. We also generated a novel Visium HD spatial transcriptomic atlas of mouse fourth-ventricle ChP to orthogonally validate epithelial modules. Lastly, cross-tissue analyses revealed substantial transcriptional overlap between ChP and retinal pigment epithelium, including shared epithelial genes and OTX2-associated regulatory relationships. Together, these findings define conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial specialization, nominate candidate regulators for functional investigation, and provide an integrated cross-species and spatial resource for studying ChP physiology.

papers.title: Olfactory Deficits and Structural Anomalies of the Peripheral Olfactory System in 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
papers.abstract: Background: Approximately 25% of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) develop a psychotic disorder, and the syndrome shares key neurodevelopmental features with psychosis in the general population. The olfactory system develops early in utero, providing a window into gestational disruptions relevant to psychosis risk. We hypothesized that 22q11DS would show impairments in olfactory function and structural anomalies of the olfactory system relative to psychosis spectrum (PS) youth without a known genetic syndrome and typically developing controls (TD). Methods: Participants included individuals with 22q11DS (n=101), PS (n=56), and TD (n=52). Sinonasal symptoms, odor identification, and discrimination (Sniffin' Sticks) behaviorally. Structural 3T MRI measured olfactory bulb volume, sulcus depth, and sulcus length. Sample sizes vary per analysis. Results: Relative to TD, 22q11DS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001), lower odor identification (p<.001), and lower odor discrimination (p<.001). PS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001) and marginally lower odor identification (p=.06), but no discrimination deficit. Olfactory bulb volume was significantly smaller in 22q11DS versus TD (p=.007, r=.39); PS showed a non-significant trend (p=.07). Olfactory sulcus depth (p=.52) and length (p=.82) did not differ across groups. Conclusions: 22q11DS is associated with elevated sinonasal burden, robust olfactory identification and discrimination deficits exceeding those of PS and reduced olfactory bulb volume. The co-occurrence of functional deficits and reduced bulb volume without sulcal anomalies may distinguish the 22q11DS olfactory phenotype from that of PS. These hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with partially dissociable neurodevelopmental mechanisms and support the utility of 22q11DS as a genetic model for psychosis risk.

papers.title: Identifying neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness and deviance using a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm
papers.abstract: The relationship between neural processes supporting perception, deviance processing, and post-perceptual task demands during auditory processing is not well understood. We used multitone masking and a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm to dissociate neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness, deviance processing, and task demands. Evoked responses to physically identical target-tone pairs were recorded across three phases differing only in task instructions. In Phase A, human participants remained nave to (and thus unaware of) the target tones. In Phase B, participants were informed about (and thus aware of) the target tones. In Phase C, participants remained aware of the target tones and judged the duration of the silent gap between them, rendering them task-relevant. When participants were aware of them, target tones elicited an auditory awareness negativity and an increased positivity in the P3 window), with larger responses when target tones were additionally task-relevant. Furthermore, though largest in Phase C, deviant stimuli elicited a mismatch negativity across all task conditions, while a significant P3 to deviants was only observed in Phase C. Thus, early and late responses can be independently modulated by awareness, deviance, and task-relevance, indicating that they do not necessarily rely on shared neural mechanisms despite overlapping spatiotemporal profiles.

papers.title: Beyond the attractor: closed-loop stimulation design for learning multistable neural dynamics
papers.abstract: Online identification of nonlinear dynamical systems faces two challenges. Noisy, partial observations make the latent state difficult to estimate. Local attractors can also keep passive trajectories in regions that reveal little about the unknown dynamics. Both challenges commonly arise in closed-loop neural experiments where stimulation must be chosen from noisy spike counts, while neural activity may remain near a stable state unless stimulation drives it elsewhere. We address this problem by actively selecting inputs to collect informative observations during the experiment. We introduce PALDI (Planning-based Active Latent Dynamics Identification), which combines extended-Kalman state prediction, single-step Laplace state updates, blockwise Gaussian parameter updates, and finite-horizon planning. Its parameter expected-information-gain surrogate combines dynamics sensitivity with state Fisher information and discounts apparent parameter information when latent states are uncertain. We compare PALDI with nonadaptive inputs, a myopic policy, and two active baselines: the one-step D-optimal method FLEX and receding-horizon curiosity with uncertainty sampling. On a bistable Wilson-Cowan model of excitatory and inhibitory populations, PALDI approaches the true-model reference and remains strongest as the observation signal-to-noise ratio decreases or the readout geometry becomes biased. We then test identification in a spiking decision network where we use a reduced dynamics and observation model to approximate the data-generating process. PALDI reaches a median held-out prediction R2 of 0.90, close to a fitted reference, and its model gives the highest change-of-mind success among identification policies. Information-guided finite-horizon planning is a practical strategy for identifying neural circuit dynamics with closed-loop stimulation.

papers.title: Cerebral hemodynamics and cytochrome c oxidase in hypoxic-ischemic rabbit fetuses
papers.abstract: Background: Understanding fetal brain responses to hypoxia-ischemia is of growing interest, as it remains unclear to what extent these responses differ from those of newborns and whether developmental adaptations during gestation contribute to such differences. Materials and methods: Using a combination of broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) and diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS), we measured brain microvascular oxygen saturation (StO2), total hemoglobin concentration (THC), relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF), and the oxidation state of cytochrome c oxidase (oxCCO) during an acute ischemic challenge in the brains of five rabbit fetuses in utero. Simultaneous measurements were acquired from four control fetuses located in the contralateral uterine horn. Results: During the hypoxia-ischemia phase, we observed a rapid reduction of CBF (47% +/- 29%) and StO2, (from 64.7% +/- 1.5% at baseline to 40.6% +/- 2.0%) together with an increase of oxCCO (3.7 uM +/- 0.5 uM). Conclusion: The simultaneous increase in oxCCO and decrease in rCBF and StO2 during hypoxia-ischemia reveals a cerebral response pattern that differs from that commonly reported in the newborn brain. These findings support the hypothesis that unique developmental adaptations influence fetal cerebral metabolism during hypoxic-ischemic stress.

papers.title: Impaired Control Symptoms in Alcohol Use Disorder Show Convergent Associations Across Behavioral and Neural Markers of Inhibitory Control and Drinking Behavior
papers.abstract: Background: Deficits in inhibitory control are considered a central feature of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet behavioral and neuroimaging findings have been inconsistent. One potential explanation is the marked heterogeneity of AUD, which encompasses multiple symptom dimensions that may differ in their underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. In this study, we investigated whether behavioral and neural markers of inhibitory control are associated with specific DSM-5 AUD symptom domains. Methods: A total of 589 participants (432 with non-treatment seeking AUD, 157 controls) completed a Stop-Signal Task (SST) during fMRI. Associations between DSM-5 symptom domains (impaired control over alcohol use, risky use, social problems, physical dependence) and SST performance, inhibition-related brain activation, and alcohol consumption were examined. Real-life drinking behavior was additionally assessed over 12 months using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Results: Greater impaired control symptom severity was associated with poorer performance on go trials and diminished post-error slowing during SST. At the neural level, higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with reduced activation across fronto-insular, parietal, cingulate, supplementary motor, and cerebellar regions. In contrast, other symptom domains showed little to no associations with inhibition-related behavioral or neural measures. Higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with greater alcohol consumption across questionnaire-based and EMA-based assessments. Conclusions: In this large cohort, altered behavioral performance and recruitment of inhibition-related brain regions in the SST was selectively linked to impaired control symptoms. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-based approaches for understanding heterogeneity in addiction and may inform the development of more targeted interventions.

papers.title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
papers.abstract: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

papers.title: Absence of the Earths magnetic field activates stress-related brain circuits in a mammal
papers.abstract: The Earths magnetic field is a constantly available cue for animals with a magnetic sense. While magnetic navigation is best studied in migratory birds, a magnetic sense is also found in some mammals. Among these, it is most thoroughly studied in African mole-rats of the genus Fukomys, subterranean mammals that navigate in kilometre-long dark tunnel systems. Our understanding of the neural pathways involved in magnetoreception remains incomplete. To address this, we here performed an unbiased whole-brain screen for magnetically induced neuronal activity in the mole-rat brain. We set up MoBI-DisC (Mole-rat Brain Imaging with iDISCO and ClearMap), an experimental pipeline that combines global c-Fos immunolabelling, tissue clearing, light-sheet microscopy, and mapping to a novel 3D brain atlas. To identify brain areas involved in magnetosensation, we exposed mole-rats to a changing magnetic field and compared their brain activity to that of control animals exposed to a near-zero magnetic field. Unexpectedly, we found that the near-zero magnetic field exposure activated many brain areas, predominantly those involved in stress and anxiety responses. These included the amygdala, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, the substantia innominata, and the periaqueductal grey. This suggests that magnetic field deprivation acts as a physiological stressor in mole-rats. To test this, we conducted a place-preference test and found that mole-rats avoid entering a zone with a near-zero magnetic field, consistent with the hypothesis that this condition is not neutral for these animals. In summary, we present a novel pipeline for unbiased mapping of neural activity in subterranean mole-rats and uncover evidence of stress and avoidance responses to the absence of an Earth-strength magnetic field.

papers.title: When Time Online Tells Us Little: Duration of Social Media Use does not Influence Sleep Disruption or Psychopathology in Adolescents
papers.abstract: Background: Adolescent mental health problems have risen alongside increasing sleep disruption and widespread social media use (SMU). However, the mechanisms linking these factors remain unclear. This study concurrently examined objectively measured sleep and SMU in relation to psychopathology to test whether SMU moderates the sleep-mental health association and to characterize day-to-day bidirectional relations among sleep, affect, mood, and SMU during the school year. Methods: Eighty-five adolescents (ages 12-18) completed 14 days of wrist actigraphy, smartphone-based ecological momentary assessments of mood and affect, and objective SMU duration tracking. Cross-sectional models tested whether SMU moderated associations between sleep and psychopathology, and multilevel daily models examined within-person lagged associations among sleep, SMU, and affect, controlling for age and sex. False discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Shorter average sleep duration and greater variability in sleep duration between weekdays and weekends were associated with higher psychopathology symptoms, primarily externalizing problems. SMU duration neither moderated nor directly predicted psychopathology or sleep. Within-person analyses showed that longer-than-usual sleep predicted more positive and less negative affect and lower next-day SMU, though these associations did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusions: Sleep disruption showed consistent associations with adolescent psychopathology, whereas the amount of time spent on social media did not. These findings suggest that duration-based measures of SMU may incompletely capture adolescents digital experiences and highlight the need for more granular, context-sensitive indicators of online behavior in understanding youth mental health.

papers.title: NREM sleep microarchitecture is associated with internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning in early adolescence
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most prior work relies on subjective measures and does not capture underlying neural processes. We examined whether alterations in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep oscillations are present in children with anxiety disorders and whether these features relate to internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning. Methods: Children aged 9-13 years with diagnosed anxiety disorders (ANX; n = 17) and typically developing non-psychiatric comparison participants (NC; n = 26) completed overnight polysomnography. Slow oscillations (SO) and slow and fast sleep spindles were characterized using validated automated detection algorithms. Participants also completed a pre-sleep emotional processing task, and parents provided standardized measures of youth mental health. Group differences and dimensional associations between NREM oscillations, internalizing symptoms, and behavioral indices of emotional processing were examined. Results: Sleep architecture did not differ between groups. Slow spindle duration was shorter in the ANX group. Across the full sample, shorter slow spindle duration was associated with greater internalizing symptoms, whereas higher SO density was positively associated with internalizing symptoms. Children in the ANX group exhibited greater facial emotional arousal and more frequent look-away behavior during the emotional processing task. Across participants, greater emotional arousal and look-away behavior were associated with shorter spindle duration during subsequent sleep. Conclusions: Specific features of NREM microarchitecture were associated with individual differences in internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning during early adolescence. These findings highlight the potential relevance of NREM oscillations for understanding developmental links between sleep and youth psychopathology.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

papers.title: A perturbation atlas of mouse neural organoids resolves macroglial reactivity and nominates drivers of degeneration
papers.abstract: Understanding neuro-glial roles in homeostasis and disease requires scalable central nervous system (CNS) models, particularly as macroglia like astrocytes and Muller glia remain challenging to study in slow-developing human systems. Here, we generate and map the cellular diversity of mouse neural organoids spanning multiple brain regions and the retina. Benchmarking transcriptomic maturation against in vivo references captures postnatal neuro-macroglial states within a month. We show that macroglia are highly responsive to inflammatory cues and adopt specific transcriptomic states also found in vivo. Through a single-cell perturbation screen targeting 13 Muller-glia-specific pathways, we map how certain inflammatory cytokines drive degeneration-like stress programs in photoreceptors and distinct reactive states in Muller glia, including an Oncostatin M-driven chaperone-associated state. Mechanistically, we identify gp130-STAT3 signaling as a targetable driver of macroglial reactivity and photoreceptor distress. Together, these single-cell atlases provide a foundation for dissecting cellular crosstalk and neuro-glial pathology in the mature CNS.

papers.title: Whole-brain receptor markers and hub excitabilities determine acute and long-term outcomes in stroke
papers.abstract: Following a stroke, changes in receptor systems have been observed that may influence the excitability of affected brain regions and drive recovery trajectories. Translating results from animal studies to patients remains a major challenge, and while imaging modalities have provided a wealth of findings, a mechanistic link between local receptor systems and observed imaging data is still missing. To bridge this gap, we built patient-specific digital twins with their own neuromodulatory profiles: we integrated 19 receptor and transporter density maps into a mechanistic whole-brain model, and estimated their influence on cortical excitability for each stroke patient and how these systems subsequently explain recovery trajectories. We found that distinct receptor profiles modulated excitability in perilesional versus non-perilesional tissue. Favourable acute motor outcomes were most strongly explained by increased inhibition mediated by non-perilesional GABA-A receptors, together with enhanced excitability driven by cannabinoid, histaminergic, and noradrenergic systems. For acute language outcomes, we identified receptor signatures that, together with motor findings, formed two cross-domain clusters linking excitability to either better or poorer performance. Remarkably, structurally highly connected hubs played a key role: their acute excitability explained cognitive and language deficits and predicted language recovery at one year. Together, our results establish a mechanistic link between receptor-specific modulation of cortical excitability and behavioural recovery, highlighting potential targets for pharmacological and non-invasive therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Mitochondrial NAD+ import gates neuronal resilience to active SARM1
papers.abstract: SARM1 is an inducible NADase that executes pathological axon degeneration, but how NAD+ destruction causes neuronal failure remains unclear. Because SARM1 is predicted to act outside the mitochondrial matrix, cytosolic NAD+ loss has been viewed as the critical lethal lesion. We show that SARM1 activation rapidly depletes cytosolic and mitochondrial NAD+ and collapses ATP in both compartments, revealing early, coupled metabolic failure. Enhancing mitochondrial NAD+ import through SLC25A51, the mitochondrial NAD+ transporter, preserves mitochondrial NAD+, maintains mitochondrial function, and delays axon degeneration and neuronal death despite ongoing SARM1 activity. Unexpectedly, SLC25A51 restores cytosolic NAD+-dependent metabolism, reversing a glycolytic block and increasing NAD+ synthesis during stress. Glycolytic inhibition attenuates protection, identifying cytosolic metabolic recovery as an important component of neuronal resilience. AAV-SLC25A51 improves function in a chronic SARM1-dependent neuropathy model. Thus, mitochondrial NAD+ import gates SARM1-driven degeneration by limiting coupled mitochondrial-cytosolic metabolic failure, presenting a downstream intervention point for axon preservation.

papers.title: DAP12-deficient microglia adopt a TREM2-independent antigen-presenting state with a glial-to-neuronal cascade in Nasu-Hakola disease
papers.abstract: Nasu-Hakola disease (NHD), a dementia with about 200 cases worldwide, is caused by loss-of-function mutation of TYROBP, encoding DAP12, or its receptor TREM2. TREM2-DAP12 is the switch that converts microglia from a surveillant to a reactive state; what DAP12-deficient microglia become and to what extent they reshape their microenvironment is unknown. We profiled prefrontal cortex and hippocampus from an NHD donor and control by single-nucleus RNA sequencing and mapped the glial changes in situ by spatial transcriptomics. NHD microglia adopted a CIITA-driven, MHC class II-high antigen-presenting state with complement, iron and glycolytic programs and Fc receptors but not the TREM2-dependent lipid program. Astrocytes became pan-reactive and lost metallothionein expression, oligodendrocytes lost mature cells and cholesterol synthesis, and excitatory neurons lost presynaptic and activity programs, consistently between regions and across a published cohort. DAP12 deficiency left microglia in an antigen-presenting state short of the TREM2-dependent arm, accompanied by a glial-to-neuronal cascade.

papers.title: Oligodendrocyte ER-phagy Restricts Excessive Myelination by Degrading Sphingolipid Synthases
papers.abstract: Myelination is critical for nervous system function. Numerous signaling pathways have been identified that promote myelin sheath growth, disruption of which can lead to hypomyelination, characterized by a reduction in myelin sheath thickness. However, the negative regulators of myelin sheath expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a cellular brake on central nervous system myelination that restricts myelin sheath thickness during brain development. This brake is mediated by a selective form of autophagy, known as endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-phagy, which degrades the ER and its resident sphingolipid synthases. ER-phagy is highly active in oligodendrocytes during myelin membrane expansion, and its impairment leads to ER accumulation, elevated sphingolipid production, and excessive myelin thickening. Genetic reduction of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis in the ER rescues the hypermyelination phenotype caused by ER-phagy disruption. In summary, our findings establish ER-phagy as a key regulator of sphingolipid metabolism and reveal a mechanistic link between ER homeostasis and myelin production by oligodendrocytes, providing insight into mechanisms underlying pathological hypermyelination.

papers.title: Serotonin2A receptors in the medial prefrontal cortex do not drive DOI-induced head-twitch responses in rodents
papers.abstract: Background The head-twitch response (HTR) is a serotonin2A receptor (5-HT2AR) dependent behavioral correlate of serotonergic psychedelic action in rodent models. Although cortical 5-HT2ARs have been implicated in HTRs, the contribution of specific cortical circuits to this behavior remains poorly defined, with a few reports implicating the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in the generation of HTRs. Results The serotonergic psychedelic, 2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI), induced head-twitch responses (HTRs) in male and female rats and mice, with sex differences noted only in mice. DOI also increased ear-scratch responses (ESRs), and reduced digging and grooming behaviors only in mice. While the DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs were absent in 5-HT2AR knock-out (5-HT2AR KO) mice, reduced digging and grooming occurred in both wild-type and 5-HT2AR KO mice. We assessed the role of 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC in regulating DOI-induced HTRs using pharmacological and genetic approaches. Targeted DOI microinfusion into the mPFC did not induce HTRs in rats, in contrast to the robust increase in HTRs noted following systemic DOI administration. Local delivery of the selective 5-HT2AR antagonist, MDL100907, into the mPFC also had no effect on the systemic DOI-evoked increase in HTRs in rats. Experiments capitalizing on genetic strategies to perturb 5-HT2AR expression in the mPFC, indicated that viral restoration of 5-HT2AR expression in mPFC CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons was not sufficient to reinstate DOI-evoked HTRs or ESRs in 5-HT2AR KO mice. Further, conditional 5-HT2AR deletion in CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons in the mPFC did not alter systemic DOI-induced HTRs and ESRs in mice. Conclusions These findings indicate that the serotonergic psychedelic DOI induces species- and sex-specific behavioral effects in rodent models, with a robust 5-HT2AR dependence noted for DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs. Further, we show that 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC do not appear to contribute to the enhanced HTRs and ESRs elicited by DOI.

papers.title: Simultaneous recordings link intracranial and scalp correlates of somatosensory awareness in humans
papers.abstract: The electrophysiological events underlying the conscious perception of touch in humans remain elusive. Scalp-EEG studies have identified a negative deflection peaking 120-200 ms after stimulus onset, known as the N140. This component, recently reinterpreted as the somatosensory awareness negativity (N140/SAN), has been proposed as a putative marker of tactile awareness, but its underlying neuronal dynamics are still unknown. Intracranial studies have shown that responses to median nerve stimulation include, after an initial phasic activation mainly localized to primary somatosensory cortices, a predominantly insulo-opercular tonic broadband high-frequency activity (BHA; 50-150 Hz) that has been linked to tactile awareness. Yet these scalp and intracranial signatures have never been directly linked. Using simultaneous high-density scalp EEG and intracranial EEG recordings, we show that the N140/SAN is the scalp manifestation of the insulo-opercular local field potential that follows the BHA response to stimulation. By bridging invasive and non-invasive recordings our results identify the neural origins of the N140/SAN and connect scalp and intracranial correlates of somatosensory awareness.

papers.title: Autonomic neurons are intrinsically hyperexcitable in a Friedreich ataxia iPSC model
papers.abstract: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an inherited multisystem disorder caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene and consequent frataxin deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration and heart disease. Clinical studies have documented autonomic dysfunction in FRDA, including elevated resting heart rate, raised plasma catecholamines and a high burden of urinary, bowel and sexual symptoms. Consistent with this, autopsy studies show degeneration of the cardiac conduction system and its associated ganglia in FRDA. Whether these features are intrinsic to FRDA autonomic neurons has been untestable without a human cellular model. Here, a human model of FRDA autonomic neurons was established by differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from individuals with FRDA and from their CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. FRDA autonomic neurons expressed canonical autonomic lineage markers and retained reduced FXN mRNA and frataxin protein levels. Electrophysiological analysis revealed pronounced hyperexcitability, with an approximately five-fold increase in spike number, shortened interspike intervals, and longer bursts. FRDA autonomic neurons also exhibited increased cell death, elevated mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and a shift from networked to tubular mitochondrial morphology. Bulk RNA sequencing of all three isogenic pairs revealed loss of extracellular matrix programs and activation of stress response pathways. The top differentially expressed gene was MEG3, a maternally imprinted long noncoding RNA, which was consistently upregulated across all three isogenic pairs. MEG3 sits within the imprinted 14q32 DLK1-DIO3 locus, whose maternally expressed noncoding transcripts were co-ordinately de-repressed in FRDA autonomic neurons. Competitive gene-set testing of 43 imprinted genes across 20 domains showed this to be specific to 14q32: no other imprinted domain was co-ordinately altered. Together, these findings establish hyperexcitability of autonomic neurons as a cell autonomous consequence of frataxin deficiency, accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction. This provides a cellular basis for the increased sympathetic tone observed in clinical studies.

papers.title: Raf-MEK-ERK signaling mediates FLT3-induced mechanical allodynia and reduced morphine analgesic efficacy in male rodents
papers.abstract: The cytokine FL and its receptor, Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), contribute to chronic pain and to the maladaptive effects of morphine but the intracellular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the contribution of the Raf-MEK-ERK pathway to FLT3dependent nociceptive signaling and to the modulation of morphine analgesia. Using HEK293T cells expressing human or mouse FLT3, primary dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, and rodent models, we examined ERK activation, TRPV1 sensitization, and behavioral responses following FLT3 activation by its ligand, FL. FL induced concentration-dependent ERK phosphorylation through FLT3, while pharmacological inhibition of FLT3, Raf, or MEK reduced this response. In primary DRG neurons, MEK inhibition attenuated FLinduced potentiation of capsaicin-evoked calcium responses, supporting a role for MEK-ERK signaling in TRPV1 sensitization. In vivo, intrathecal FL increased ERK phosphorylation in DRGs and induced mechanical hypersensitivity, both of which were reduced by Raf or MEK inhibition. In FLT3/MOR-expressing cells, morphine potentiated FL-induced ERK activation, an effect reduced by naloxone and abolished by FLT3 inhibition. In rats, MEK inhibition prevented the FL-induced reduction of morphine analgesia and subsequent mechanical hypersensitivity. Together, these findings identify Raf-MEK-ERK signaling as an important downstream pathway linking neuronal FLT3 activation to nociceptor sensitization and impaired morphine analgesic efficacy.

papers.title: An Engineering Explanation of Human Vertical Reaching: Optimal Trajectory Planning of Asymmetric Velocity Profiles in the Vertical Plane via a Softplus-Based Generalized Dynamic Jerk Cost Function.
papers.abstract: The results in this article demonstrate that the central nervous system CNS plans trajectories in the vertical plane by minimizing a Generalized Dynamic Jerk GJerk cost function, which we have proposed as an advancement of the traditional Minimum Jerk cost function. While the traditional Jerk cost function generates smooth trajectories by minimizing the third derivative of joint angle over time, it neglects real dynamic constraints most notably the effect of gravity. According to our engineering interpretation, the arm functions as a constrained manipulator where gravity acts as a non-linear, state-dependent bias; thus, the asymmetry in velocity profiles is not an anomaly but an optimal adaptation to the gravitational field. Consequently, it predicts mathematically symmetrical upward and downward movements, even in contexts where gravitational forces play a decisive role. The proposed GJerk cost function extends the classical framework by incorporating position-dependent dynamic coefficients into the cost function, thereby embedding gravitational effects directly within the planning process. As a result, the generated movements are not only smooth in a mathematical sense but also physically and mechanically consistent with the actual torque and energy demands imposed by the musculoskeletal system. The GJerk cost function reduces angular change in high-gravitational-torque regions because it makes the joint configuration with the highest gravitational torque more expensive within the cost function, prompting the planner to choose a slower and more conservative movement. This does not physically dissipate energy, but it acts as a behavioral damping mechanism, similar to how humans naturally slow down when approaching a high load or potentially dangerous configuration. In this way, the GJerk cost function reduces abrupt changes in joint kinetic energy and prevents sudden jumps in acceleration, ultimately producing a smoother and more stable trajectory that aligns with both biomechanical reality and observed human behavior. Within this framework, upward movements become inherently more costly than downward ones, penalizing configurations that require large torques to counteract gravity. This induces a biomechanically meaningful asymmetry, ensuring the resulting trajectories reflect the body's true mechanical constraints rather than mere geometric smoothness. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GJerk cost function provides a more realistic and physiologically grounded account of motor planning in the vertical plane, linking smoothness optimization with genuine dynamic requirements and offering a closer approximation to biological motor behavior

papers.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
papers.abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

papers.title: The Onset of Breathing at Birth Switches Off Regenerative Capacity
papers.abstract: Many mammalian tissues, including the central nervous system (CNS), lose regenerative capacity in adulthood, but when and how this transition is initiated remains unclear. By monitoring mTOR activity, an evolutionarily conserved readout of cellular growth and intrinsic regenerative potential, we found that mTOR signaling declines within minutes after birth in murine CNS neurons and in other organs such as the heart and skeletal muscles. Focusing on retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), we show that this abrupt decline is driven primarily by CO2 exhalation following the onset of breathing after birth. Using real-time in vivo imaging of RGCs during the earliest postnatal period, we further discover that breathing-induced CO2 exhalation rapidly causes intracellular alkalinization, activates an AMPK-family kinase, SNF-related kinase (SNRK), which in turn suppresses mTOR signaling. Importantly, this process remains reversible in adulthood: CO2 inhalation or Snrk deletion restores mTOR activity in RGCs and enables robust regeneration of their axons after injury. Similar CO2 inhalation-induced mTOR reactivation occurs across multiple cell types and organs, suggesting a general mechanism by which breathing-associated CO2/pH signaling shapes the regenerative capacity across life and pointing to a potential CO2-based strategy for promoting tissue regeneration.
